span.label: Verbal multiword expressions - verbal idioms - and the relation between their semantic properties and the syntactic variation they permit.
span.quote: In this chapter we focus on verbal MWEs, often referred to as "verbal idioms" or simply "idioms".

span.label: Is the behaviour of idioms an idiosyncratic property of each idiom, or a consequence of more general constraints?
span.quote: Our primary research question is whether the behavior of idioms is an idiosyncratic property of each idiom or a consequence of more general constraints.

span.label: Replaces decomposability with an alternative categorization that cross-classifies idioms on two dimensions, figuration and transparency.
span.quote: In this chapter we consider an alternative categorization of idioms. More precisely, we cross-classify idioms according to two dimensions: figuration and transparency

span.label: critique
span.quote: we argue that decomposability is not a primitive semantic property of idioms, nor can it be used to predict idioms' behavior.

span.label: idiom flexibility is a continuum rather than a two-way split, with every idiom examined showing some flexibility
span.quote: we hypothesize that idioms cannot be categorically classified as either flexible or rigid. Rather, we envision a continuum with idioms exhibiting varying degrees of flexibility, possibly dependent on their semantic properties.

span.label: corpus study
span.quote: We used heTenTen 2014 (Baroni et al. 2009), a billion-token web-crawled Hebrew corpus, available on SketchEngine (Kilgarriff et al. 2004), to search for different types of variations that occur with representative MWEs from the three semantic classes we outlined in Section 3.1. We focused on fifteen specific verbal MWEs, and annotated 400 examples overall.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the idiom whose common characterization is rigidity is searched for in a twenty-billion-word corpus, chosen because the earlier corpora were too small to distinguish an idiom that cannot vary from one that is simply too rare for its variants to appear
span.quote: In order to verify that the idiom's common characterization as a rigid idiom is not an epiphenomenon of its low frequency, we consulted a much larger corpus: enTenTen13 (Baroni et al. 2009), a 20 billion word English corpus, available on SketchEngine (Kilgarriff et al. 2004).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: idioms are cross-classified on two dimensions at once - figuration, whether a literal meaning can be pictured, and transparency, whether the route from that picture to the idiomatic meaning can be recovered - in place of the single decomposable/non-decomposable cut
span.quote: In this chapter we consider an alternative categorization of idioms. More precisely, we cross-classify idioms according to two dimensions: figuration and transparency. Figuration reflects the degree to which the idiom can be assigned a literal meaning. Transparency (or opacity) relates to how easy it is to recover the motivation for an idiom's use, or, in other words, to explain the relationship between its literal meaning and its idiomatic one.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: queries are written in a corpus query language over morphological features - part of speech, lemma, clitic - combined with logical operators, which the authors call particularly important for casting a wide net over non-canonical word orders, discontinuous elements and morphological inflections
span.quote: SketchEngines's Corpus Query Language (CQL) provides a way of defining complex queries which target morphological features of words (e.g., POS, lemmas, clitics) and which make use of logical operators (and/or/not). These features are particularly important when our goal is to cast a wide net to retrieve variations in general, and in particular non-canonical word orders, discontinuous elements and various morphological inflections.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: a query wide enough to catch variants also returns results that are not instances of the idiom, so each result is inspected by hand to remove the false positives
span.quote: Nevertheless, a wide net comes at a cost; not all the retrieved results are necessarily instances of the idiom. Often, only a manual inspection of each result can weed out the false positives.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the endpoint is switched from frequency to existence: rather than how often each variation occurs, the study verifies that every type of variation occurs at least once for each idiom
span.quote: For this reason we do not present quantitative data with regard to the distribution of the canonical idiom and its variations. We did, however, verify the occurrence of all types of variation for each idiom.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: argument-structure variation is observable in Hebrew because it is carried by combining one consonantal root with different morphological templates
span.quote: Hebrew presents an interesting case in this respect, since argument structure variations are associated with the combination of one consonantal root with different morphological templates (Doron 2008; 2003).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the modifier question is split in two: modifications of all types count as variations, while it is the modifier's semantic SCOPE that can provide evidence about whether idiom parts are assigned individual idiomatic meanings
span.quote: The question of whether a modifier is internal or external relates to the issue of decomposability, but not to the question of flexibility. When idiom parts are syntactically modified in an idiom this is certainly an instance of variation; the idiom does not appear in its canonical form. Thus, modifications of all types are variations. The semantic scope of the modifier can provide evidence with respect to whether idiom parts are assigned individual idiomatic meanings or not.

span.label: The study reports no quantitative distribution, because the wide-net queries return false positives that only manual inspection can remove.
span.note: what this limits: any rate or distribution of canonical versus variant forms from this study: the authors state they do not present quantitative data, and why
span.quote: Nevertheless, a wide net comes at a cost; not all the retrieved results are necessarily instances of the idiom. Often, only a manual inspection of each result can weed out the false positives. For this reason we do not present quantitative data with regard to the distribution of the canonical idiom and its variations.

span.label: The generalisation rests on a limited set of Hebrew verbal idioms.
span.note: what this limits: cross-linguistic or general claims about idiom flexibility: the authors bound the generalisation to a limited set of Hebrew verbal idioms
span.quote: Naturally, this generalization, which is based on our work on only a limited set of Hebrew verbal idioms, requires further investigation.

span.label: The criterion under critique is described as impressionistic and circular: flexibility is taken as evidence for the very property meant to predict it.
span.note: what this limits: decomposability as an independent predictor of flexibility: the paper states the diagnosis is prone to circularity with the behaviour it predicts
span.quote: determining whether an idiom is decomposable or not is rather impressionistic, and is prone to circularity, where its flexibility is taken as evidence for its decomposability.

span.label: The originating proposal supplied neither precise definitions of its two categories nor a procedure for telling them apart.
span.note: what this limits: the decomposable/non-decomposable split as an operationalised classification: no definitions or decision procedure were given with it
span.quote: Nunberg et al. (1994) do not provide precise definitions for the two categories, or a specific procedure for distinguishing between them.

span.label: An independent corpus study classifying by paraphrase reported the boundary between the two categories as fuzzy.
span.note: what this limits: the decomposable/non-decomposable assignment as sharp: the study that applied it reports the boundary as fuzzy
span.quote: She classified those for which she found an appropriate paraphrase as decomposable. Nevertheless, she observed that the boundary between the two categories is fuzzy.

span.label: Two psycholinguistic studies of the same construct disagree on whether speakers can apply it reliably.

span.quote: In contrast, Titone & Connine (1994) did not find reliable agreement regarding decomposability in their study. Of the 171 idioms which they examined, only 40% were classified into one 38 2 Verbal multiword expressions: Idiomaticity and flexibility of the three categories (normally decomposable, abnormally decomposable nondecomposable) with at least 75% agreement among subjects. The authors suggest that grouping idioms into these categories may rely on a type of linguistic knowledge that is not easily accessed.

span.label: The rigidity of the field's standard example is shown to depend on corpus size; variation appears only in a very large corpus.
span.note: what this limits: the canonical rigidity of kick the bucket: variation is attestable only in very large corpora, so earlier rigid classifications may reflect corpus size
span.quote: However, since this idiom is used relatively rarely and idiom variations in and of themselves are relatively infrequent, non-canonical instances of it and other infrequent idioms can only be empirically attested in very large corpora. This, we believe, is an important methodological finding, which at this point in time, with the availability of large annotated corpora, cannot be overlooked.

span.label: The authors' own prediction about cranberry idioms was not borne out, and they say so.
span.note: what this limits: the transparency/figuration hypothesis as confirmed throughout: the cranberry class behaved opposite to the authors' stated expectation
span.quote: We were especially surprised by the behavior of the cranberry idioms. Our initial expectation was that the lack of transparency and figuration would render these idioms more rigid. Our corpus findings, however, reveal a different picture.

span.label: Neither proposed dimension accounts for idiom behaviour on its own; the paper attributes the effect to an interaction.
span.note: what this limits: transparency or figuration singly as a predictor of flexibility: the paper states neither alone accounts for the behaviour
span.quote: Thus, we propose that neither transparency nor figuration alone can account for the behavior of idioms. Our findings suggest that there is an interaction between the two dimensions.

span.label: the rigidity claim was re-checked against a much larger corpus, enTenTen13
span.note: eliminates: that the idiom looks rigid only because it is RARE - that its apparent fixedness is an artefact of low frequency in a small corpus
span.quote: In order to verify that the idiom's common characterization as a rigid idiom is not an epiphenomenon of its low frequency, we consulted a much larger corpus: enTenTen13 (Baroni et al.

span.label: cranberry idioms
span.quote: Among these idioms we find what are referred to as "cranberry idioms" (Moon 1998; Trawinski et al. 2008), which, similarly to "cranberry morphemes", have parts which have no meanings

span.label: transformational deficiency
span.quote: they are known to exhibit "transformational deficiencies" (Chafe 1968: 111), such as resistance to passivization, modification and topicalization.

span.label: decomposability - Nunberg et al.'s sense: an idiom whose meaning, once known, can be distributed among its parts
span.quote: The former are idioms whose meaning, once known, can be distributed among their parts. A typical example is spill the beans, where spill roughly means `reveal' and beans roughly means `secrets'.

span.label: transparency - the relation between an idiom's literal and idiomatic meaning, which the source proposal explicitly warns must not be confused with decomposability
span.quote: They do however explicitly warn against confusing decomposability with transparency, which they define as the relation between the literal and idiomatic meaning.

span.label: paraphrasability - whether the idiom can be paraphrased by a similarly structured phrase, explicitly distinguished from decomposability
span.quote: An additional distinction is made between decomposability and paraphrasability. The fact that the meaning of an idiom can be paraphrased using a phrase of a similar argument structure does not necessarily indicate that it is decomposable.

span.label: flexibility - the categorical sense inherited from Nunberg et al., on which an idiom is either transformationally productive or transformationally deficient
span.quote: They propose that the semantic distinction between decomposable and non-decomposable idioms accounts for the difference between "transformationally productive" and "transformationally deficient" idioms.

span.label: flexibility - this paper's sense: a continuum, with idioms exhibiting varying degrees rather than falling into two classes
span.quote: Rather, we envision a continuum with idioms exhibiting varying degrees of flexibility, possibly dependent on their semantic properties.

span.label: figuration - the degree to which the idiom can be assigned a literal meaning that conjures a picture
span.quote: Figuration reflects the degree to which the idiom can be assigned a literal meaning. Transparency (or opacity) relates to how easy it is to recover the motivation for an idiom's use, or, in other words, to explain the relationship between its literal meaning and its idiomatic one.

span.label: critiques → Nunberg et al. (1994)
span.note: differs in: WHICH PROPERTY DETERMINES FLEXIBILITY, AND THE CHALLENGE IS MOUNTED ON TWO SEPARATE GROUNDS THE PAPER NUMBERS ITSELF: 'FIRST DUE TO THE FUZZINESS OF THE NOTION OF DECOMPOSABILITY, and SECOND, in light of empirical investigations in English and in other languages that revealed FLEXIBILITY WITHIN IDIOMS PREVIOUSLY CLASSIFIED AS NON-DECOMPOSABLE.' One ground is about the criterion being unusable, the other about it being wrong where it is usable - and the replacement offered is a pair of graded dimensions, transparency and figuration, rather than a sharper version of the same binary
span.quote: We challenge Nunberg et al.'s (1994) proposal, attributing decomposability as the determining factor regarding idioms' flexibility/rigidity, first due to the fuzziness of the notion of decomposability, and second, in light of empirical investigations in English and in other languages that revealed flexibility within idioms previously classified as non-decomposable.

span.label: critiques → Nunberg et al. (1994)
span.note: differs in: WHETHER THE CRITERION CAN BE APPLIED INDEPENDENTLY OF WHAT IT PREDICTS. 'determining whether an idiom is decomposable or not is rather IMPRESSIONISTIC, and is PRONE TO CIRCULARITY, WHERE ITS FLEXIBILITY IS TAKEN AS EVIDENCE FOR ITS DECOMPOSABILITY' - so the property that is supposed to PREDICT flexibility is in practice read OFF flexibility
span.quote: The dimension which Nunberg et al. (1994: 498) assume plays a crucial role in determining the behavior of an idiom is its decomposability. Nevertheless, as was previously mentioned, determining whether an idiom is decomposable or not is rather impressionistic, and is prone to circularity, where its flexibility is taken as evidence for its decomposability.

span.label: critiques → Nunberg et al. (1994)
span.note: differs in: WHICH WAY THE IMPLICATION RUNS. Decomposability was proposed as 'the semantic property of idioms which PREDICTS their behavior', but 'at times THIS HYPOTHESIS IS TURNED AROUND and idiom flexibility is used as A DEFINING PROPERTY of non-decomposable idioms' - the predictor becomes the definition, at which point the hypothesis cannot fail
span.quote: In this chapter we challenge the validity of the hypothesized correlation between decomposability and flexibility. As previously mentioned, decomposability is a fuzzy notion which is difficult to apply when classifying idioms. Although it 40 2 Verbal multiword expressions: Idiomaticity and flexibility was proposed by Nunberg et al. (1994) to be the semantic property of idioms which predicts their behavior, at times this hypothesis is turned around and idiom flexibility is used as a defining property of non-decomposable idioms.

span.label: qualifies → Riehemann (2001)
span.note: differs in: WHETHER A FUZZY BOUNDARY BLOCKS A CLEAR RESULT. Riehemann classified idioms by whether a similarly structured paraphrase could be found, 'NEVERTHELESS, SHE OBSERVED THAT THE BOUNDARY BETWEEN THE TWO CATEGORIES IS FUZZY. This notwithstanding, her findings show a CLEAR DISTINCTION' - canonical forms accounting for about 75% of occurrences of decomposable idioms against 97% of non-decomposable ones. A classification its own author calls fuzzy still separates the data

span.quote: We propose an alternative classification that builds on the notions of transparency and figuration. We hypothesize that the more transparent and figurative an idiom is, the more likely it is to be "transformationally productive".

span.label: Idioms are not uniformly rigid; some keep their idiomatic meaning outside their canonical form.
span.quote: Not all idioms, however, are equally rigid, as some maintain their idiomatic meaning even when they do not appear in their canonical form.
